title: Islamic golden age debunked: the borrowed brilliance behind Baghdad's glory
hook: Discover how the so-called Islamic Golden Age was built on lost libraries and borrowed ideas.
description:
Discover how the so-called Islamic Golden Age was built on lost libraries and borrowed ideas. This short unpacks the myths behind the era's true legacy.

Subscribe for more myth-busting history in under a minute.
#IslamicGoldenAge #HistoryMyths #Baghdad #history #historyfacts #shorts

beats.say: You think the Islamic Golden Age was a nonstop parade of invention, but the truth flickers.
In 750, the Abbasids seized Baghdad, yet the city's libraries burned twice before knowledge truly blossomed.
The famed House of Wisdom opened under Caliph al-Mansur, but it relied on earlier Persian scholars rescued from Sassanid ruins.
Al-Kindi's logic thrived only because Greek texts survived the 8th-century Byzantine embargo, not from original Arab insight.
When scholars translated Aristotle in 823, they omitted his physics, leaving a gap later filled by European Renaissance.
The 9th-century astronomer al-Biruni mapped the Indian Ocean, yet his data vanished after the 1258 Mongol sack.
Baghdad's 10,000-book library burned in 1258, erasing half the era's scientific records in a single night.
Meanwhile, thriving hospitals in Cairo and Cordoba saved lives, but their techniques were copied from earlier Greek manuals.
By the 12th century, Europe imported Arabic numerals, yet the numeral system itself originated in India centuries before.
So the 'Golden Age' was a patchwork of borrowed brilliance, not a solitary Arab miracle.
